segments.text: begin by quoting from your book, The India Way in 2020, in which you said, the formula ahead was engage America, manage China, cultivate Europe, and reassure Europe.
These are daunting challenges.
As you look back over the past six years since you wrote that book, how do you see at all even a whiffing semblance of symmetry between these four what look to be contradictions per se?
Thank you.
Thank you very much.
And let me say what a privilege, what an honor it is to be back here at the Cotelia Economic Conclave.
And you said that we had commonalities.
I want to make it very clear I'm actually emulating Georgia.
He was foreign minister before me.
He was author before me.
So I had the great privilege of being High Commissioner when he was foreign minister in Singapore.
So it's really a great pleasure, a delight to see you back in India and be on the same panel.
I would like to make two points, one of course in response to your question and the other in a way in response to the theme of this conclave and the theme of this panel.
The first, the point, you know, how do you do what I said we should be doing with all those countries is in a way what we would today call multi-alignment.

which is we have partners who each have their interests, each of these relationships is different, they have a different history, they have different challenges, they have different opportunities, different possibilities and that
there was a time when you could say that was an issue unique to India.
I think more and more countries today face that, which is how do you engage all the players in the world, all the important players in the world at the same time?
And where you don't, I would argue that actually it is to the detriment of the country itself.
So at this time, where the US is concerned, it is, as with many other countries, it is one of our principal strategic partners.
It is our largest economic account.
It's our biggest trade account.
It's a very major critical defense partner.
And what happens in an era – and that's the bit which I want to come back to later, which is what you call an age of flux, I think, is the – so in an age of flux, how do you deal with the U.S.?
How do you deal with the rise of China?
How do you respond to a much more, I would say, stable, traditional relationship with Russia?
And how do you explore new possibilities with Europe, where we have actually concluded an FDA and hoping that it would be – and not just with Europe, but the UK as well?
So I think each one of these today offers possibilities, I'll be honest.
Many of them have their challenges.
Because we have challenges, we shouldn't have a black and white view of that relationship.
We have to weigh it in a very considered and judicious way.
And given India's perspective, I would argue that actually every relationship net-net is a plus for us.
And therefore we should really have the confidence of pushing ahead on every front.
Knowing that progress on any front makes it easier on other fronts.
So it's a kind of the opposite of a zero-zero sum game.
If I can just add one final word, this whole conference is themed as resilience in an age of flux.
I think that itself tells us a lot.
It's a description today of the times we are in and the fact that we focus on resilience as the key attribute also tells us
I mean it is at the end of the day an evaluation by us collectively of what this age of flux is about.
And where this panel is about, the title of it is adaptive by design.
So, clearly, your expectation is in this age of flux when we are looking for resilience, how do we adapt to these changing circumstances?
How do we customize for the challenges and for the relationship and for the problems?
And that is really today what we are occupied in in foreign policy.
Thank you.
Thank you, Jaishankar, for those observations explaining and linking it up to the broad theme of this Kautilya.

Turning to you, George Yu, and you are also such a prolific writer as Yashanka himself conceded that you had perhaps taken to writing much more aggressively much before he began, but I quote from your own book.
You said in your musings, too, you have written several parts of musings.
I have had the pleasure of reading most parts of your musings.
You said something very interesting, which to some extent does in a way comment on the last part of Minister Jashanka's remark.
You said in that musing, China, and I quote from your book, China is not interested
impacts Sinica because it involves a lot of work.
That's what you said in 23.
Given the developments of the last three years, as you are talking in 2026, would you still say that many people who have argued that China is seeking to replicate a G2
That is somewhat at variance with China's lack of interest in being Pax Sinica.
How have you seen the evolution since you wrote your musings too?
I don't think China likes to be described as being in the G2 of the U.S.
because that puts it in an uncomfortable position.
It will become the biggest economy on earth.
It will be a very powerful country.
But the mentality of the people throughout its history is to build walls around themselves.
In a crisis, the foreigners leave.
Their own people stay.
Sometimes they're not allowed to leave.
When the crisis is over, the foreigners come back.
It is, unlike India, an unusually homogeneous society.
Over 90% of the people are Han.
There's only one written language.
There's only one literature.
There's only one set of heroes.
And because of this, there's a deep instinct to present homogeneity.
And I don't think they're very comfortable with foreigners.
I go to China very often.
I must have been there over 100 times in the last 40 years.
I've watched it develop.
I visit the tourism sites.

To be a foreigner standing in line, it's kind of an inconvenience to them, you know, because they all have their cards, they're zipping through, and there they look at your passport, they look at you, and they have to record some things.
It's okay.
A few foreigners, like garnishes on a dish, that's fine.
But I don't think they would ever want Beijing and Shanghai to be like New York and London.
That's not what they want.
But there is a need for society.
And because of that, they don't want to get involved in other people's affairs.
You see, I have enough problems of my own.
I wish you well, but thank you.
Thank you.
Turning to you back again, you have just come back from a triumphant visit, certainly a very successful visit.
from the UN General Assembly.
You addressed the UN General Assembly.
You addressed the Asia society.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, you did talk of the difficulties and challenges of four P's, which are well-known, food fertilizer and energy.
And so you have also said, throw away the old playbook, because you expect a new geometry.
like to share with us what you see are the contours of that new geometry which may be still in the process of evolution?
Well, I wouldn't say it was a triumphant visit.
I'm not even sure.
I mean, I might settle for a successful on a good day, but it certainly was a very

very arduous visit but the point here, I mean in a way it's a, I would say, I don't want to say it's a contrast but let's say it's expressing an Indian personality here on the international stage that a lot of the concerns which we voiced
were concerns of other people, of other countries.
They were also our concerns, but if you look, I mean, at the foref, for example, food, fuel, fertilizer, finance, these were much more the concerns of many global south countries.
For us, fuel prices, the cost of fuel has gone up.
We have absorbed it.
Our diplomacy has driven very hard to make fuel accessible by increasing the number of sources in the middle of a crisis.
We have increased our fertilizer procurement so that you don't have a fertilizer problem in this country.

So actually if you look at it from a very narrow national Indian perspective, for us fuel costs are high, fertilizer costs have gone up, but what I was really expressing was a larger sentiment and a larger interest of the global south.
because the Global South does expect a country like India to go up on that stage and articulate it.
Somebody has to do it.
And that somebody in the eyes of many countries, at least one of the somebody's is a country like India.
The reason why in a way a new architecture or as you called it a new geometry is coming into being is because we have today the alliance, the old alliance structures have loosened up at least.
The rise of China has in a way created new compulsions and new responses out of the international system.
There is already a rebalancing happening.
Many other economies have risen.
Rising economies have naturally accompanying political influences.
So we are moving towards a multipolar world whose architecture and geometry is obviously very different from the way it used to be before.
That is the age of flux that this conclave is looking at.
And in this,
I think a country like India, one part of it, the big countries which you referred to in your first question, are relationships that we need to manage.
But we also, as a post-colonial society, have a very strong emotional bond with the global south.

They have equally an expectation of India that as the largest country, the most populous country as the biggest economy of the global south that we would stand up for the rights and the concerns of the global south.
And I think that's this I would say being there for the rest of the world is very much I would argue ingrained in the Indian approach to the world.
that we may be, we are in many ways unique, but we are not distant from the world.
So we are very connected and we feel that obligation to build that into our foreign policy.
NK, may I reinforce this point?
Yes, but could you do so in the context of the other question, which is completely consistent with your earlier observation,
that when you gave the example of standing in a line and so on, you have in an earlier musing said that China has a different interpretation.
Rule by law does not mean rule by the rule of law.
It's different than believing in the rule of law.
And that, therefore, is that a characteristic which would be an important factor in shaping the diplomatic and geopolitical outlook forward?
In the context of that, you could also make the observation which you have planned to make now.
Please, George.
I think India and China study in contrast and similarity.
We have very strong family structures.
So at the level of the family of relationships, it is very easy for us to understand each other.
From the viewpoint of statecraft, China has always been very unique because of its long civilization and the continuity of that civilization.
And it's not easy, I think, for foreigners to fully understand China.
Whereas India, if you look at the map, the old world, India is smack right in the middle.
And the Indian Ocean is not at the Pacific or the Atlantic, which only came to prominence after the new world was discovered.
So India has always been where
The winds blew six months in one direction, six months in the other, where there's constant mixing of cultures, of people, of spices, of everything.
So India, in a sense, reflects.

reflects the diversity of the world all around the Indian Ocean Rim and it gives people a sense of comfort or familiarity when they come to India in a way which they may not feel when they go to China because in China you feel that I'm non-Chinese, I'm a foreigner in a homogeneous sea.
But in India you can always find nature's comfort zones for yourself.
And I must say India has positioned itself very well.
To begin with, it is not threatening to the other major powers the way China is.
And Minister Jayashankar in the government has been very skillful in positioning India in that sweet spot.
It's not static.
It's dynamic.
It must keep on shifting.
But India maximizes that position.
It doesn't threaten.
So others wish India well.
In Southeast Asia, we want India to grow.
We want our trade with India to grow because we are finding our dependence to China, while good for us, a little too imbalanced.
Japan wants India to do well.
Europe wants India to do well.
So to the U.S., if nothing else but to counterbalance China.
So India is able to play to this strength and the fact that there is a huge internal market which is growing
year by year means that everyone wants to have an equity stake in India.
And in the Kautilya dialogue, this acceleration in the future is palpable.
Thank you.
Mr. Jayashankar, yesterday one has been kept following your speeches, speaking to the

to the Munich conference, you did mention about some possible changes which might take place on this whole Ukraine-Russia situation, the Black Sea and so on, which would have enormous implications in terms of the security of supply, restoring credible supply chains.
How do you see India's role
in the entire issue of the evolving dynamics of the ongoing, hopefully, a meaningful dialogue between Russia and Ukraine.
Well, what I – I mean, I'd be happy to kind of replicate or perhaps dwell upon those observations.
You know, from the very start, we have always held that this conflict in Ukraine is unlikely to be resolved in the battlefield.
And therefore, it was important to have negotiations between the parties.
And that dialogue and diplomacy was probably the best pathway.
Now, there were actually negotiations in the early stages of the conflict.
To some extent, there have been negotiations on different aspects of that conflict, limited issues of that conflict.

What has also happened during this period is that many of the parts as an engine of growth, which historically we have known has stood countries well, would like to comment on what you see as some of the immediate concerns over the next 12 months to 12 to 24 months in India being able to sustain its current growth trajectory and its current macroeconomic stability.
Well, I think much of that was answered by Nirmala Ji when she spoke here.
But I would only add to that that for India today, you know, our early free trade agreements were with the ASEAN, with the ASEAN countries individually, collectively, with Japan, with South Korea.
So it is, I think it was imperative to
have a balance and really open out to countries where the markets are more transparent, where actually more mature, where the purchasing power is greater.
And I would say, you know, suddenly from a diplomatic perspective, I do regard the EU FTA
the UK FTA, the EFTA TEPA, what we have done with two of the Gulf countries, UAE and Oman, and hope to do with the GCC in entirety, the trade agreement that we are negotiating with the United States,
To me, these are big steps with great possibilities which would have a truly beneficial impact on the economy and also to my mind provide a balance to what we had done in an earlier era.
Thank you, George.
Any closing comments on the broad theme?
of today's discussion in any form or the other of the discussion?
The essence of trade is it is voluntary.
You cannot be forced to trade.
I trade because it benefits me and you trade because it benefits you.
And from time to time, there will be disputes.
So there must always be dispute settlement mechanism, enforcement of contract, arbitration.
In the case of WTO, we have tribunals.
They are critical to the WTO.
But the US has decided to block the appointment of judges to WTO tribunals.
So this has effectively rendered the WTO mechanism ineffective.
The result is a group of companies, including Europe, have come together to say, look, OK, the US doesn't want to appoint judges, but we will now create tribunals for ourselves.
So we look back in history, arrangements at the Hanseatic League.
We are part of the league.
You subscribe to its dispute settlement mechanism.

In all future agreements between ASEAN and India, between India and Europe, there are dispute settlement mechanisms, which means there is a predictability to which trade can take place and all parties can benefit.
And in the world we're entering, I think the world of the past is past.
There are still many ways in which we can benefit each other.
And if we concentrate on our own self-interest, I think we will find arrangements which will be mutually beneficial.
And if we can draw more people into the bargain, the greater the sum will be positively.
Thank you, Mr. Jaishankar.
Any closing comments which you would like to make?
Well, I've seen some of what the earlier speakers, including my ministerial colleague, has said at this forum.
And what I want to say today is, as a foreign minister today, for us, when we look at
our national development pathway, the goals we are following.
The ability, the right to industrialize, the ability to industrialize, to develop particularly advanced manufacturing of getting a fair deal for our agriculture.
of ensuring that we are protected from unfair competition, of widening our market access particularly vis-a-vis many of the more developed economies.
These are today, there has been a much tighter linkage in the last decade between foreign policy and the economic and development goals of this country.
And so what I would say is, you know, we see, again, as people who spent a lifetime in the government, a lot of your ability to execute things depend on coordination.
The coordination today between my ministry, finance, commerce, some of the other line ministries who have important economic responsibilities is really much, much tighter than I've ever seen.
before and we know that this is going to be this age of flux as you call it is going to be a turbulent one.
It will be volatile.
There will be uncertainties.
We are seeing two major conflicts.
We are seeing other frictions.
As I said there is the pressure of nonmarket factors.
There is the tariff volatility.

So taking all of this into account, yes, these are choppy waters, but I think as our record shows, we've been able to rise to the challenge, whether it's the COVID challenge, whether it's the challenge today of a double conflict.

the challenges of energy, of food, of fertilizer and you know we need to factor that into our thinking, plan for it and respond to it and that is really I would say in a sense the task before us and I am very confident we will rise to that challenge.
Well, thank you very much, Minister Jayashankar and Mr. George Yu.
Thank you for this closing session.
And if I may say so, on a somewhat anecdotal note, that Minister Jayashankar knows that this is the fifth year of the Kautilya economic conclave.
Time has gone.
We have always had the pleasure
of having Minister Jaishanka to give the closing plenary, which has really greatly enriched the quality of the Kautilya economic conclave.
We thank you profoundly for this gesture, and we hope that with your continued support, we will be able to move forward and forge better alliances.
Thank you so much for this opportunity.
Thank you.
I request you all to please remain seated
Thank you.
parties which have an interest, will not be directly fighting, they have actually stopped dealing with each other.
And one of the problems when you have that is if there is no contact and both sides are surmising what the motives and the
behavior is of the other, that doesn't help to infuse confidence.
Now in this particular case, though we have been maintaining for some time that both parties should

come to the table and, you know, there were a number of conferences where countries gathered to express their support for peace but often they would gather in the absence of Russia and we always felt, you know, what is the point of having a gathering dealing with the Ukraine conflict where Russia is not there?
So in this particular case what happened was that in the month of July there were attacks on civilian shipping by both Russia and Ukraine.
And in the course of those attacks, some Indian sailors were killed, some were injured.
And we find, you know, we regard these attacks as completely unacceptable, whether it is in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, or the Gulf.
So we protested very strongly to the Russians, to the Ukrainians.
I myself took it up with the foreign ministers of both countries.
And we started getting active initially to secure the maritime shipping and the mariners involved in that.

Now those conversations brought out the nature of the cargo which was being carried by the ship and there was the concern expressed about the grain exports which had come to a halt, pretty much come to a halt in the Black Sea.
So the conversation developed into whether non-attack on shipping is good, but is there a possibility of facilitating the shipment of grain?
And the problem was that shipment of grain in the conversation was not seen as a – to be dealt with as an isolated issue.
So it got linked to energy.
So it became a somewhat broader conversation.
So those conversations are ongoing at this time.
Prime Minister met President Putin in Bishkek.
And after that, he asked me to go to Kiev.
I went to Kiev and met President Zelensky and my counterpart, Foreign Minister Andrei Sebiha.
Then I came back and reported to PM.
President Putin was in Delhi for the BRICS.
And they had a further conversation.
And we still keep in touch with both sides.
So I think this is still something we have to see.
It's not obviously an easy situation.
It's not something which is anybody can say with a high degree of confidence that something is going to come up.
But it seems definitely an effort worth making because, as I said, we do feel the global south's concern.
You know, if grain exports from Black Sea stop, it's going to affect international
grain market.
If energy exports stop, again it's going to disproportionately impact the global south.
If fertilizer exports stop, the same thing would happen.
So of course we have our interest but more than our interest we also have the larger interest of the global south and frankly we have the interest of the parties themselves.
that, you know, that if they can even agree on something of a limited nature, we feel that in the given circumstance that's a big positive.
All right.
Two more questions given the shortage of time and this I will ask you and request also George to comment on this question depending on Minister Jaishanka's reply.
Jaishanka, you have just come back from
the United Nations General Assembly.
Today's is the broader question of the entire international financial architecture which is in deep disarray.
Multilateral institutions are crumbling.
In one form or the other, this morning we had a conclusion was that there does not seem to be an immediate prospect or revival of trade as a mechanism of growth in a credible way.
Looking at the broader picture, could I request you to comment on the future of the United Nations?
in terms of the principles and objectives which it had been laid down at the end of the Second World War.
And what do you see coming from the UN last meeting of the UN General Assembly?

And given all the other uncertainties, including the kind of leadership which may come at the end of the term of the present Secretary General of the UN, what in your view is the future of the UN, and as a sub-question,
the future of multilateral institutions in the world.
Yeshanka.
Thank you.
Well, where the UN is concerned, I think it's obvious to everybody by now that the UN is gridlocked.

that if you look at the big issues of the day, whether you look at the conflict in the Gulf, whether you look at the conflict in Ukraine, whether you look at other issues in Africa, whether you look at the COVID, actually the United Nations has been largely irrelevant to the decision-making.
I think, again, there's a widely held view that a lot of it is because the Security Council is gridlocked and that the Security Council no longer represents the entirety of
the global interest.
The UN started with 51 members.
It's got almost four times that number today.
So, you know, if you have grown four times and you want to keep the old board of management, it's not going to work.
I mean, it's common sense.
Now, the problem is there are a few players, a few countries who are resistant to the reform of UN.
And they are using the name of Africa.
They're using Africa's interest as an argument to block the reform of UN.
And the irony is Africa actually now has a clear position.
Africa has actually come to the intergovernmental negotiations and indicated what they would like to see.
They have laid out their position.
So I think we need to see whether we will continue to watch, in a sense, the irrelevance or the, I would say, ineffectiveness is a better word, of the UN.
And it's an important question, because we need the UN.
The UN has done a big service to the international community.
Our job must be to fix the UN, not to work around the UN.
But the UN itself has to help with that process.
So, but the other question on the international financial architecture, I'll give you a larger answer.
I do think not just the financial system, but more important, the trade system.
There's a widespread feeling in the world that the system is broke, that at the heart of the issue is we created a system for market which is based on market principles.
And we today have very substantial non-market practices which
have not been called out and the non-market practices today have distorted the international economy.
So this struggle between a market norm and the non-market reality

I think is at the heart, if today a lot of countries are going against the trading system, if they are raising, you know, if they are not playing by the rules, part of the reason is that they have a grievance that the non-market aspects of the overall trading system have become so big that, you know, playing by the rules doesn't benefit them anymore.
So the very people who invented the rules are now walking away from the rules because of the non-market practices which have advanced so drastically.
Thank you.

George, while addressing that question, could you also address the question that – which Minister Jaishankar referred to on per se, weaponizing trade, every aspect of the trading being weaponized far away from the gains of trade which traditional economics has taught us?
We've all been used to a world where trade, investments, finance, health management were all depoliticized.
And that was because after the end of the Second World War, the U.S.
was so dominant, the institutions which served us well were in fact under a pucks Americana.
the Bretton Woods institutions, the UN, WTO, WHO.
In recent years, the U.S.
has decided that those institutions no longer serve its own interests, and in some cases, left them, like the WHO, or undermined them, like the WTO.
We may need another global cataclysm.
before restructuring takes place.
That is the reality of global power.
Because to effect change, you need some kind of consensus.
It will be jammed.
And the U.S.
is not helping.
But maybe if we look back in history, trade, finance have always been politicized, have always been recognized.
And to some extent, we are returning to that world.
I think the important thing for the future is we look after our own regions and where we can with fellow travelers with whom we share a kindred spirit.
I find it interesting that on many key issues like on Ukraine, like on international institutions, China and India in fact have identical positions.
And while the structures appear to be collapsing, if India and China stand up together, I think many structures will hold.
I mean, the WTO can continue without the U.S., the WHO is continuing without the U.S., the UN after a fashion, and then we need to create regional or plurilateral structures as a supplement.
So in Southeast Asia, we have ASEAN.
And we have the ASEAN constellation of arrangements which bring in other powers.
And in this way, within ASEAN, we create an architecture of stability for ourselves.
I think India will do the same.
And maybe ASEAN and India together can do much more.
And India, ASEAN, and China can work together, which is more than half the world.
and the faster growing half can do a lot for global stability?
Well, I think that there could be wide variations of opinion on that, but that ASEAN issue complicates it.
The issue of how to improve the matrix of Indo-China relationship

can be taken independent of bringing the ASEAN together, I'm sure that Minister Jayashankar, who has also been our distinguished ambassador to China, would see it equally in a broader historical perspective.

All efforts are on, including a very minor one, incidentally, which occupies considerable space in newspapers on the possibility of some flight routes being taken to cut short the flying time in case the Chinese airspace could be used in a particular way.
But that is a sub-issue of the broader issue on which Minister Jayashankar has said several times earlier.

that you cannot overlook the fact that till there is a degree of trust and comfort on the issues of border in a certain way, it's possible to make independently enormous progress on the other aspects of it.
Minister Jashankar would like to comment on that.
I wouldn't like to comment on what you said, but I'd like to comment on what George said.
We can't seriously look at the global trading system without the United States.
is such a major trading power and is the biggest economy.
So I think in many ways the idea that, you know, a few countries come together and then try to fix the problem because the U.S.
is a problem, I don't think that's a viable option.
Secondly, I don't think the U.S., I mean, we can't say trade.
U.S.
is to blame for all the trade problems.
Lot of the market distortions which have come in the trading system have not come from the US.
Some have.
But lot of them have come from other sources.
So I would say, you know, we need to be very sort of objective about where the problems are today for the trading system.
I mean, look at it from India's point of view.
I look at where I'm running big deficits, and it's not the deficit per se I have a problem.
I have a problem on the deficit because it reflects a market constriction, a market access restriction.
So these are problems which need to be looked at.
So I can see that there may be a kind of a, you know, in a sense, political narrative about Asian countries coming together.
But I think there's the reality of the global economy, there's the reality of market practices and non-market practices, and we need to fix that.
Okay, I think that one last question to both of you.

What do you think that therefore, Minister, would be the very immediate daunting challenges which the Indian economy faces as an engine of growth, considering the fact that notwithstanding your comment on what is happening in Asia,
and the sort of little thing that we have in the United States.
What about the new bilateral investment trade agreements, which will give a great Philip to trade, which hopefully will act as a growth impulse of using trade as an interactive, free conversation.
Let me begin with you.
Let me begin by quoting from your book, The India Way in 2020, in which you said, the formula ahead was engage America, manage China, cultivate Europe, and reassure Europe.
These are daunting challenges.
As you look back over the past six years since you wrote that book, how do you see at all even a whiffing semblance of symmetry between these four what look to be contradictions per se?
Jai Shankar.
Thank you.
Thank you very much and let me say what a privilege, what an honor it is to be back here at the Cotelia Economic Conclave.
And you said that we had commonalities.
I want to make it very clear, I'm actually emulating Giorgio.
He was foreign minister before me.
He was author before me.
So I had the great privilege of being High Commissioner when he was foreign minister in Singapore.
So it's really a great pleasure, a delight to see you back in India and be on the same panel.
I would like to make two points, one of course in response to your question, and the other in a way in response to the theme of this conclave and the theme of this panel.
The first point, how do you do what I said we should be doing with all those countries, is in a way what we would today call multi-alignment.

which is we have partners who each have their interests, each of these relationships is different, they have a different history, they have different challenges, they have different opportunities, different possibilities and that
There was a time when you could say that was an issue unique to India.
I think more and more countries today face that, which is how do you engage all the players in the world, all the important players in the world at the same time.
And where you don't, I would argue that actually it is to the detriment of the country itself.
So at this time, where the U.S.
is concerned, it is, as with many other countries, it is one of our principal strategic partners.
It is our largest economic account.
It's our biggest trade account.
It's a very major critical defense partner.

And what happens in an era and that's the bit which I want to come back to later which is what you call an age of flux I think is the – so in an age of flux how do you deal with the U.S., how do you deal with the rise of China?
How do you respond to a much more, I would say, stable, traditional relationship with Russia?
And how do you explore new possibilities with Europe, where we have actually concluded an FTA and are hoping that it would be – and not just with Europe, but the UK as well?
So I think each one of these today offers possibilities.
I'll be honest, many of them have their challenges.
Because we have challenges, we shouldn't have a black and white view of that relationship.
We have to weigh it in a very considered and judicious way.
And given India's perspective, I would argue that actually every relationship net-net is a plus for us.
And therefore, we should really have the confidence of pushing ahead on every front, knowing that progress on any front makes it easier on other fronts.
So it's kind of the opposite of a zero-sum game.
If I can just add one final word, this whole conference is themed as resilience in an age of flux.
